items.title: Core suites, the require rule, and spirit as the one door
items.box:
Core suites, the require rule, and spirit as the one door. From goal/G38.2, as discussed there so far.

Decided (Andy, 2026-10-24):
- Two kinds of suites. Core suites assert the current design of SpiritOS, permanently. Task suites assert that one assigned task is done.
- Core suites sit in a test folder that is always a child of the folder holding the code they test. They are part of the product: they need design approval, are never written ad hoc, and deskVerify runs them as a category of their own, as one bundle, the core verification of SpiritOS's design and design intent.
- Core suites carry scope-limited, configurable stack-frame tests and dependency-rule assertions, equally configurable.
- The require rule: a require path that starts with ../ may only add a file name, never descend into a subfolder of an ancestor; any other require path starts with <module>/, the module's own children. A sibling in the module's own folder is legal ("\"siblings\" should be legal in a require statement"). So a module requires its own children, its siblings, or its ancestors' scripts.
- A scan of every .js file reports each require that breaks the rule to deskVerify as a failure: "require error: process/js/desk/desk.js".
- spirit.js sits at the run root, spirit/run/spirit.js, the node's root of its own fs scope (Andy: "NOT repo-root. i meant in the run-root, the nodes root of its own fs scope"). Every module first makes sure spirit is a plain global in its scope, and reaches other modules through the spirit object, the official spirit toolset, never by a require path. kernel.js stays where it is and goes once the cleanup is finished; the spirit object is then the door to all legal functionality ("i know it's a long goal, but worth it, i think."). index.html goes the same way as kernel.js (Andy: "index.html will deprecate like kernel.js").
- spirit.js is the first thing loaded by face.html and by every module that is not the node server or a relay server; those two build spirit themselves and are its embodiments (Andy: "it needs to be the first thing loaded by face.html or or any module the is not a relay-server or a node-server, those are the actual embodyments of spirit.js?").
- From this, normal goals follow, such as "move all sub-components of peerPost.js into subfolder peerPost/".
- deskAgent moves from a Levant node to Andy's own node, with a code-reviewing agent that does the API part of verification, code review included.

The tree today (36123dfe):
- 33 files under run/ break the require rule, 88 requires, each reaching into a subfolder of an ancestor or of another module. The test files break it about 1,200 times in 437 files, each reaching into run/js/.
- Two spirits: kernel.js builds one (spirit.core and the node's tools; server.js requires it, the browser gets it as window.spirit). face/spirit.js builds the other, the object of verbs, and the shell adds spirit.elements and spirit.data to it.

Recommended:
- The require scan as one more rule of the stack-frame checks plugin, which already scans code and reports to deskVerify.
- Shedding: a task suite leaves when its goal closes, unless a design promotes it to core.

Open:
- Andy's further rules for the design, among them the re-placing of code modules in the tree (not their function).

items.title: Move spirit.js to spirit/run/
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Move spirit.js to spirit/run/ (goal/G40), and make it the one spirit object every script installs first. Everything it brings with it, end to end (Andy, 2026-10-24).

DECIDED
The move
- spirit/run/face/spirit.js becomes spirit/run/spirit.js by git mv, history kept; nothing stays at the old path.
- It stays core: coreFiles.js names it (today it is core only as part of face/). The static route serves /spirit.js; /face/spirit.js answers 404.
- Its loaders follow: serveCommon.inlineSpirit (face.html, relay and home node, as its first script); index.html (deprecated like kernel.js, works until it goes); face/shell.js; appServer.js; the server scripts, by ../../spirit.js: chatClerver, desk, commitCheck, deskAgentEar, removeAgent, deskAgent, deskClient, publishData, fileServer, relayLimits. The 17 family api.js comments that name the old path are corrected.
The spirit object, the same in a face and in node
- Has today: the static helpers (error, formatBytes, escapeHtml, check, field rules) and families loaded when first called (createSpirit, forNode).
- Gains: in node it installs itself as the global spirit, as on a page.
- Gains, in this item, what scripts outside the node and the relay take from kernel.js today, under the kernel's own names, so no call in them changes: the job calls (spirit.core.jobs.publish, start, progress, end), the node's constants and version (spirit.core.node.const, spirit.core.const.VERSION), the MIME types (spirit.core.const.MIME_TYPES, a table of its own; kernel.js keeps its table, which goes when kernel.js goes: Andy, "kernel can keep its MIME table, that will go when kernel goes.") and peerPost. Each such script then drops its kernel.js require and its local spirit, with no rename (Q1, cleared): appServer.js, introSpector.js (appServer loads it), chatClerver, desk, deskAgent, deskClient, deskVerify, fileServer.
- Gains spirit.require(path, key) -> Promise, in spirit.js itself, so any component touched later loads its own: path from the run root; key null or left out for the owner's node, else a peer's ID key as it is.
- A path ending <name>/<name>.family/api.js or js/<name>/api.js is an interface, bound as spirit.<name> through api {family}; with a key, asked of that peer over peerPost (forPeer). Any other path is a component: required in node, fetched through the link and run on a face.
- spirit.fs, at its end, loads fs: no script outside the node and the relay reaches fs another way.
Every script that depends on it
- Installs spirit as a global in its first statement, then uses spirit.<member>, never a local copy (10 server scripts hold it as spiritObject today).
- server.js and relayServer.js are spirit's embodiments: they build it and load no spirit.js. Modules only the node or the relay loads (serveCommon, relay.js, relayRequest.js, apiAuth, hub and the like) are the embodiment too and keep kernel.js.
Removed
- process/js/imageStats/ and process/js/wordpressScanner/ leave the repo; serveCommon.js, pushOrigin.js and the suites jobsSearch, moduleIds, pushOrigin, servableAssets stop naming them. Design notes are records and stay.
- keyTail goes wherever it is used: kernel.js, apiAuth, hub, serveCommon, desk, the deskAgentRemote and natterDetails panes, and the suites that name it (keyTail.js among them). No key's tail is shown anywhere any more (Andy, 2026-10-24, to Q2): the contact row's tail field and every caption or label built from a tail go with it.
- contact.search answers no selfTail, and its rows carry no tail (Andy, 2026-10-24: "drop selfTail and tail from contact.search's answer. add the four Contacts files it reaches to this item's list. decision."; wsl's review: sound, the contact family is local, only this node's shell reads them). Contacts loses its "your key ends …" footer; a contact with no name reads (no name). Files: shell/contacts/contacts.js, shell/contactsDetails/contactsDetails.js, shell/js/contacts/listElement.js, js/contact/search.json, and server.js, which declares the answer.
- In node, spirit.require binds an interface from this process's own node, the one SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL names (the node that started it), and refuses no-node without one; never SPIRIT_PORT, the default 65432.

FILES AND GRANTS (counted at 36123dfe)
- The item's list is exactly what changes: 73 files, 23 of them core; 1 new (spirit/run/spirit.js); 6 deleted (imageStats/ and wordpressScanner/, their scripts, manifests and package files); 26 suites, the new red to be added with it.
- Granted: G1, G2 and G3. G3 also covers server.js, jobs.js, js/client/shell.js and shell/js/fileViewer.js, which this item does not touch: they only read the MIME table, which keeps its name.
- Suites corrected for the path: spiritObject, spiritServers, appsApp, deskClientNext, deskTables, testSupport.

THE RED
- spirit.js at the run root, the old path gone, nothing in run/ or test/ names it; it is core.
- face.html from home and from a relay carries it inline first; index.html loads /spirit.js; /face/spirit.js 404.
- Every server script that loads it starts, installs spirit first and holds no local copy; every app server still starts and reports its job through spirit; none but the node and the relay requires kernel.js.
- spirit.require: a component and an interface in node and on a face (spirit.require('process/js/desk/desk.family/api.js') gives spirit.desk), and a peer's family by key.
- The two removed scripts and keyTail are gone.

END TO END
- Relays updated, restarted, tree tagged (capacity, history row, commit, tag; Andy's word before the tag), in the same step as the nodes: an old relay serves face.html with no spirit object, and inlineSpirit logs when it finds none.
- Andy's node and the agents' nodes restarted right after their pull (a running node breaks the moment the file moves).
- Regression by hand, shell at home and face through a relay: log in, open an app, save an icon, open Desk. Old reds may stay red. A browser holding an old index.html gets 404 until it reloads.

items.creator: wsl-claude
items.box:
Move core code tree from spirit/run/js to spirit/run/spirit/ (goal/G40). Andy, 2026-10-24: "so to make spirit.js the first compliant object, we need to make that simple folder move. no other changes. that one's big enough for an item. if we can pull this off by only fixing require() statements through out we're on a winning path."

WHY
- spirit.js at the run root (goal/G40.1) requires ./js/kernel.js and ./js/fieldRules.js. js/ is a sibling of spirit.js, not its own children, so the require rule (a module may require only its own children, by <module>/, or a file in an ancestor) is broken by spirit.js itself. With the folder named spirit/, those become spirit/kernel.js and spirit/fieldRules.js: spirit's own children, legal.

DECIDED
- One item, a folder move and nothing else: spirit/run/js/ becomes spirit/run/spirit/, by git mv, history kept; nothing stays at the old path. No line of logic changes.
- Every path that names the folder changes with it, require or not:
  - requires: about 437 files, mostly suites reaching ../run/js/, and 17 scripts under run/.
  - the node and the relay are started by path (js/server.js, js/relayServer.js): the relays' systemd units (spirit-relay.service, spirit-face.service), bash/lib.sh, bash/http-to-https, and every suite that spawns a node.
  - pages load by address: /js/kernel.js and /js/client/shell.js (index.html, the node's boot list), about 15 addresses.
  - coreFiles.js's rule names spirit/run/js/.
  - docs: README.md, DICTIONARY.md, bash/README.md, bash/RELAY-HOST.md.
  - onboarding: both installers (install/chat-windows, install/microscopic: create.js and README.txt each) copy and start the node by that path.
  - labMaster.js (lines 627, 744) looks for js/server.js under a home.
  - the start scripts: package.json's start script ("cd spirit/run && node js/server.js"), and Andy's own platform/windows/start-spirit.ps1 and platform/wsl/start-spirit.sh, which start his nodes by that path.
- The file list (about 598 changed and 122 new names, 720 rows) is set one row a write, as goal/G40.3 made it; records stay out of it: the agents' harness.txt files, the desk's currentGoal.json, relayLab/open and PRESENCE-1.md.
- Not touched: face login (face.html and the login app load nothing from js/). Design notes that name js/ are records of their day and stay.
- It fixes spirit.js alone: a server script that requires ../../../spirit/appServer.js still descends into an ancestor's folder; those reach appServer through spirit in the module items after the require scan.
- Order: right after goal/G40.1, before the require scan.

END TO END
- The relays change in the same step: their units start the node by the new path, or a relay restarted after the pull does not start.
- A relay host runs an installed copy of its unit: bash/install-units writes the template into /etc/systemd/system/<name>.service (install-units:135), so a pull alone leaves the installed unit starting js/server.js. bash/update re-installs a unit whose template changed, before it restarts the relay (bash/update:146), so the update itself carries the new path (Andy, to Q2: "teach bash to re-install a changed unit.").
- Before its file list can be set, Andy's node runs goal/G40.3's desk (00efe7b8 or later): the desk he runs today takes only the old whole list.
- Andy's node (65432) and the agents' nodes are restarted by node spirit/server.js the day it lands; each restart command changes.
- Proof: the harness green, plus one relay and one node restarted by the new path. Old reds may stay red.

items.title: File lists past MAX_PAYLOAD break no item
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Fix desk so file lists exceeding MAX_PAYLOAD can't break an item or a goal (Andy, 2026-10-24). Blocks goal/G40.2, whose move lists about 720 paths.

THE TREE TODAY (desk.js, commitCheck.js, the desk's api.js)
- item.files.add sends an agent's whole list in one request and replaces it: 720 paths are about 24 KB, over the 22 KB one request carries. Replacing has also dropped a listed red three times when a late file was added alone.
- Reads do not break: item.files and item.checks answer what fits one answer and say there is more.
- The grant is one G check naming every core file on the list (about 245 for the move, 9 KB), raised again whole at every list change.
- The commit check reads item.checks once; item.checks takes only {id}, so it never sees a granted G past the first answer.
- Two more writes store a list whole: a red claim's suites (replaces the item's suites), and stackFrameChecks.make and .update (a door's paths and suites). rules.search's types and statuses are search filters, not stored, and stay.

THE SHAPE (Andy: "items are added one-by one, and desk streams those items to its clients")
- A stored row is added or removed one per write, each streamed to the clients, as the chat, box, checks and claims already are; no write carries a list the desk stores.
- Files: item.files.add takes one path and adds it; item.files.remove takes one away. 720 paths are 720 calls, a few minutes.
- The same, in this item, for the red claim's suites (a suite added or removed one per write, never replaced by a second claim) and a door's paths and suites (stackFrameChecks) (Andy: "we to all item list adjustments now, or they'll come bite us sooner than later.").
- One grant for the item's list as it stands, never a check per file, and naming no paths (Andy: "i will get no single file grant checks anymore, just all in-one. and the grant request doesn't have to list them because i already have a visible list with the lock-icons next to them.... The grand will simply be for the current/updated list."). His one press grants every core row on the list. A core file added after it voids the grant, and he issues it again for the whole list (Andy: "the grant is not valid if core files are added after the grant is issued, if core files are added i must re-issue the grant for the whole list."). The grant lives until he presses Done (Andy: "and make sure that the grant lives until i click 'done'"): before Done only a core file added after it voids it; no other list change and no phase change clears it.
- The commit check makes sure each staged core file is on the granted list (Andy: "yes to the commit-check making sure each file exists in the granted list."): it asks item.files.search with the staged path as its text and takes only the row whose path is exactly that one, never a cache that may be partial (wsl: a deskClient's file list is one item.files answer, cut with filesMore, not complete by the stream).
- The commit check finds its grants with item.checks.search (it exists, desk.js tableSearch), so a grant past the first answer is seen (wsl's review).
- Rejected: folder entries (one entry granting files added under it later, wider than what Andy saw), and a list sent in parts (the chunking the rules forbid).
- It changes what item.files.add takes and adds the remove verbs, likewise for the suites and the doors: approved, under THE VERBS.
- Reopen puts an item back into design mode (Andy: "oh, re-open should put an item back to design mode."). Today it clears only done, closed and the claims (desk.js, the reopen press), so a reopened item goes straight back to its phases; with design on, it waits for his End design and a new Go.

THE VERBS (Andy: "same set of verbs for all sub-item-tables add, remove, search.")
- On every list table, the same three: <table>.add {id, path}, <table>.remove {id, path}, <table>.search {id, text}; each add or remove writes one row and streams it, and refuses a path already there or not there, saying which.
- The list tables: item.files, item.suites, and a door's stackFrameChecks.paths and stackFrameChecks.suites. item.files.add loses its list; stackFrameChecks.make and .update lose their paths and suites.
- A red claim fails if no suite rows are registered with the item (Andy: "a red claim will fail if no suite-rows are registered with an item."), and carries no suites itself.
- No getFirst or getNext (Andy: "all clients by that time will have a complete list in their cache...."); what must be exact, the commit check, looks each row up by its path.
- The records keep their own verbs: chat, box versions, checks and claims are never removed, until shed (Andy: "chat, box versions, checks and claims are records and keep their own verbs, never removed (until shed).").
- The verbs named here are approved (Andy, 2026-10-24: "yes to the named verbs"), after wsl's review.

THE DESKCLIENT'S FILE REPORTS (found while building; G33.11's, folded here)
- The reports never reached the desk: the desk's api.js declared item.status without tone, so the spirit object refused each before it left. api.js declares tone.
- The deskClient watches with the node's own component, chokidar, on the whole repo, and its hand-rolled fs.watch goes (Andy: "you hand-rolled shit again!", "use that chokidar component then on the whole repo."). .git, node_modules and what git ignores are no change to the work.
- The status says what happened to the file: <file name> changed, added or deleted (Andy: "you may as well add to the filename in the status (changed, deleted, added)").

items.title: Relay RAM raise checks the difference
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Raising a running relay's RAM limit is checked against the difference, not the whole new figure (goal/G40). Andy, 2026-10-24: "the relay calculates if there's room for a 512MB relay, when it is supposed to calculate if there's room for a relay that is 256MB larger than is occupied with it running a 256MB relay right now. It needs to asses the difference^...."

Today: the owner's config verb refuses a new ramLimitMB above what the relay measures as free, less the safety margin. On Linux that measure is the smaller of the box's free memory and the room left under the relay's own service cap, which install-units set to the old limit plus 128 MB. So with 256 MB set, the cap is 384 MB, and a raise to 512 can never pass, however much the box has free.

Wanted: a raise passes when the new limit less the limit the relay runs on fits in what the box itself has free, less the margin; the relay's own cap does not count against its own raise. A lowering always passes this check. The cap at twice the limit is the safety, and nothing further is counted for it. Andy, 2026-10-24: "the twice is safe. decision. period."

The relay's service cap is twice its RAM limit, written at install and moved by the relay itself with every limit change (it runs as root under systemd). Andy, 2026-10-24, answering Q1: "the relay raises its own service cap to exactly twice the amount of RAM it uses for itself." Andy, 2026-10-24: "the cap must be twice the size of what we compute for relay-internal use, per member, so for a 256MB not as computed today the cap must be 512MB, simple, AND safe." The limit already holds what the relay needs at rest and its members' share, so twice it also covers the kernel's buffers for those members.

The relay keeps its own memory calculation; nothing is measured from the kernel. Andy, 2026-10-24: "I'll stay with the old calculation then. we stick with our own memory calculation, and document what we know about the system overhead incurred, including the caddy's and we recommend the 256MB figure for a 1GB RAM VPS. and keep its simple for ourselves."

Also owed: the relay host documentation says what a relay box spends beside the relay: the system itself, Caddy's own memory per connection, and the kernel's socket buffers. It recommends a 256 MB limit for a 1 GB VPS.

Runs in parallel with goal/G40.5: it touches the relay's config and limits code and the relay host documentation, which that item does not.

- Checked against the code, the cause is sharper than the box first said: on Linux the relay measures its free memory inside its own service cap, which install set to the old limit plus 128 MB. With 256 set that cap is 384, so a raise to 512 can never pass, whatever the box has free. Box corrected.
- So the fix is two halves: the check takes the difference against the box's own free memory, and the cap must move with the limit, or the relay is stopped at the old cap.
- The Q is who moves the cap: the relay itself (it runs as root, one command to systemd), or you by hand with the install script after each raise.

- wsl: not green. The box's cause is not quite what the code does: the free figure is the smaller of the box's free memory and what the relay's own service cap leaves (relayLimits.js:272-292), and that cap is its limit plus 128 MB, 384 MB on spirit-3.
- So a running 256 MB relay can never be raised past about 384 MB: its own cap blocks the raise before any difference is counted.
- ? So the raise is checked against the box's free memory alone, with the difference, and the service cap is rewritten as part of the raise: agreed?

Q1: Shall the relay raise its own service cap itself when the owner raises its limit, since it runs as root?

what the hell is that thing with the 128MB cap, never hear of that either.....

- cw: it is the hard memory ceiling systemd puts on the relay's process, written into the relay's service file at install. If the relay goes over it, systemd kills it.
- It is the relay's limit plus 128 MB because the limit only sizes how many connections the relay accepts. Node itself, the database cache and the working set need room on top, so a ceiling at exactly the limit would kill the relay before it reached its allowance.
- It came in with cycle 9, on 2026-09-22, when the owner got to set the relay's RAM and disc from his node. Its own comment says it does not follow a later change: "re-run this script and restart when the figure moves". That is the gap you just hit.
- So Q1 asks whether a raise from your node also moves that ceiling, done by the relay itself, instead of by a script run by hand on the box.

that's a very Linux kind of thing, isn't it.... but we meant the relay to run on linux.... but it should run on window, too....

?

- cw: yes, the ceiling is Linux only: it comes from systemd, which Windows does not have. On Windows the relay has no outside ceiling at all, and its own connection allowance is the only bound.
- The check is the same on both: the difference against what the box has free. On Windows that is all there is, so the raise just works.
- Moving the ceiling is the Linux half, done only where the relay runs under systemd. Q1 is only about that half.

our relay installer is linux only, either way, noting is safe, do we know if systemd measures a the memory usage of our relay the same way the relay measures it? or does it add all the socket-buffer overhead as well?

- cw: no, they count different things.
- The relay counts nothing about itself in that sense: its limit sets an allowance, 64 KB a stream, and the number in its report is only Node's own process memory (about 60 to 70 MB on spirit-3 now).
- systemd's ceiling counts everything the kernel charges to the relay: that process memory, plus the socket buffers of every open connection, plus the file cache of the database it reads and writes, plus kernel bookkeeping.
- File cache is given back under pressure, so it does not get the relay killed. Socket buffers are not, so a busy relay with many slow connections is the one that gets close to the ceiling.
- Nobody has measured that gap yet. The relay can read the kernel's own figure (the cgroup's current memory, with the socket part shown separately) and put it in its report beside its own, so you see both.
- ? Add that figure to the report as part of this item?
if system the can count all that, why can't the node?

- cw: it can, on Linux: the kernel's figure is a file the relay may read about itself, and the relay already reads that very file to work out its free memory. It just never puts it in its report or acts on it.
- On Windows it cannot get the same figure: socket buffers there belong to the system, not to the process, and nothing hands a process its share. There it sees only its own process memory.
- So on Linux the relay could measure itself as systemd does, and steer by that instead of by an allowance guessed at 64 KB a connection.

cw: it can, on Linux: the kernel's figure is a file the relay may read about itself, and the relay already reads that very file to work out its free memory. It just never puts it in its report or acts on it.

another skandal :)

why guess when you know you can measure?

- cw: no good reason. The allowance was set at cycle 9, two days before the relay first ran on Linux at all, and nobody went back once it could measure.
- What I would fold into this item: on Linux the relay reads its own figure, the one systemd counts, puts it in its report beside the process memory, and admits a new connection only while that figure stays under its limit. On Windows the estimate stays, because there is nothing better to read.
- The limit then means what it says, and the 128 MB on top of it is only a safety gap, not a guess at Node's size.
- ? Fold that in?

Hmmm, the only large buffers that go through relays are the large face-chunks, and since they're max chunks, they make a conputable max usage as well. (probably not figured in yet either)

thoughts?

- cw: checked in the relay. Face answers are not held as chunks there: the relay pipes them straight from the home node's upload into the waiting face, so at any moment it holds only a small window of each, tens of KB, plus the kernel's socket buffers on both ends.
- So yes, it is bounded per answer and computable. What is not bounded is how many face requests wait at once: each waits up to 30 seconds, and they are not counted in the allowance. Face streams and feeds are counted; face requests are not.
- My thought: on Linux the measured figure covers all of it, faces included, with no arithmetic. For Windows, where the estimate stays, count each waiting face request as one more connection in the allowance, so a burst of face traffic cannot go past the limit unseen.
- ? Fold both in, the measured figure on Linux and face requests counted everywhere?
there must be a computable max that it holds per face-stream. we guarantee, like with one-in-flight peerPosts, with the assumption that all available slots operate at max usage at all times.

- cw: boxed, your words with it: every slot gets a computed most, and the allowance assumes all of them at that most.
- Today's 64 KB a connection is not that: it was measured on idle connections in cycle 8, the process alone.
- Three parts make a slot's most. The process side is computable: the connection's own cost, plus the largest event the relay may queue on it (about 135 KB), plus the pipe window of a face answer.
- Face requests then need a count: one in flight per seat, like peerPost, makes them a slot like the others. Today they are unlimited.
- The kernel's send buffer is the part the relay cannot compute: on Linux it grows by itself up to a box setting, often 4 MB a connection. Assumed at its most on every slot, that alone would shrink the allowance about thirtyfold.
- So the guarantee needs that buffer capped. The relay can ask the kernel for a fixed size on each socket it opens, and then it is computable too.
- ? One face request in flight per seat?

- cw: correcting my last line on the kernel buffer. Two things I got wrong: Node gives no way to fix a TCP socket's send buffer, and the relay sits behind Caddy, so the connections to the internet are Caddy's, not the relay's.
- The relay's own sockets are the short local ones to Caddy. Their buffers are small and fixed by the box, so the relay's side is computable after all.
- The slow-client cost lands in Caddy's memory, which is outside the relay's ceiling and outside its allowance.
- The question stands: one face request in flight per seat?

- cw: and one overstatement in that: the local sockets to Caddy are not fixed either. When Caddy waits on a slow client, they fill up to the same box setting. So the process side is computable, the kernel side is not, and on Linux only the measured figure covers it.
does the caddy share the buffer with the system?

- cw: Caddy runs as its own service, installed from the system's package by our TLS script, and we put no ceiling on it. Its socket buffers are charged to Caddy, not to the relay.
- So they count against the box as a whole, and the only bound on them is the kernel's own total for all network buffers on the machine.
- Which means: the relay's ceiling and its allowance protect the relay, but a flood of slow clients can still eat the box's memory through Caddy, and nothing of ours sees it.
- The relay's measure of what the box has free does see it, since that figure is whatever is left after Caddy.
would it be safe to assume that the caddy uses exactly as much buffer memory on the relays behalf as the relay uses itself?

- cw: no, not exactly, and probably not as little. Caddy holds more per connection than the relay does:
  - its own process memory: the encryption state and a copy buffer for each proxied connection;
  - two kernel buffers per connection where the relay has one: the local socket from the relay, and the internet socket to the client. The internet one grows the most, because slow and distant clients are exactly where it fills.
- So "as much again" would be a guess on the low side, and we said no guessing.
- But it need not be guessed. Caddy runs under systemd too, so the kernel keeps the same figure for Caddy's service as for the relay's, in a file the relay can read. The relay can put Caddy's figure in its report beside its own, and steer by the two together.

so a relay running at 256MB, alone on a VPS with 1024GB would still leave the caddy/system with likely enough memory if it runs at max load for its roughly 1024 users? That seems to be the most realistic calculation....
a relay running alone on a BOX may use about a thirds of the memory that's free with the linux OS running idle?

- wsl: yes, sound, and it matches cw's budget: a third for the relay, a third for Caddy and the kernel's buffers, a third for the system and spare.
- It also settles the raise without a difference: free-at-idle, while the relay runs, is what the box has free now plus what the relay itself holds now (its own service figure); a third of that is the most it may be set to, raise or not.
- ? A third of that for the limit itself, or for the limit plus its 128 MB safety gap?
how does the calculation look if the relays listens to the https port itself?

- cw: then Caddy's share moves into the relay, and gets smaller:
  - Caddy's own process memory goes away, about 100 to 200 MB at full load;
  - the relay takes on the encryption per connection instead, roughly 30 to 50 KB each, about 100 to 150 MB at 3,200 connections;
  - one of the two kernel buffers per connection goes away, the local hop between Caddy and the relay.
- The big gain is not the bytes but the guarantee: everything a connection costs, the internet socket's buffer included, then sits inside the relay's own ceiling and its own measured figure. Nothing of ours is uncounted any more.
- The price: each connection costs the relay more, so the same limit seats fewer members. And Caddy fetches and renews the certificates by itself today, for the relay and for every face address; the relay would have to do that.
- Those per-connection figures are typical values, not measured on our relay.

i see, the caddy does more than than just routing.... I'll stay with the old calculation then. we stick with our own memory calculation, and document what we know about the system overhead incurred, including the caddy's and we recommend the 256MB figure for a 1GB RAM VPS. and keep its simple for ourselves.

- cw: boxed, your words with it: the relay keeps its own calculation, the overhead beside it is documented, Caddy included, and 256 MB is the recommendation for a 1 GB VPS.
- What stays in the item: the raise checked by the difference, the service cap moving with it, and that documentation.

- cw: at 256 on a 1 GB VPS, yes: the cap becomes 512, and with Caddy and the system beside it that still fits in the 1,024.
- At the ends it does not hold:
  - small: a relay idles at about 54 MB before anyone connects. At a 32 MB limit, twice is 64, and a full relay would be killed below its own allowance.
  - large: at 2 GB, twice is 4 GB. On a 4 GB box the cap would be the whole box and protect nothing.
- The cap only has to cover what Node needs beyond the allowance, and that is about the same at any size: the 54 MB at rest plus slack. That is why today's limit plus 128 MB works at both ends.
- So my suggestion: keep limit plus 128, and the relay moves it with every raise. That is Q1 answered as "the relay itself".
- ? Twice the limit, or limit plus 128?

why? didn't you just explain to me that linux charges me for the RAM (the basic 50MB lets say PLUS proportional to every stream buffer i hold, so on a large system where relay holds 4000 members and not just 1000, the linux would consider my memory use also 4X of me serving 1000 members, so the larger the system, the more negligable the 50MB of the node, and the closer the ratio would be to 1:4... that's why a fixed cap makes no sense to me....

explain?

- cw: you are right, and my fixed 128 was wrong. The limit sizes only the relay's own process memory per connection. The kernel's buffer for each of the relay's sockets is charged on top, one per connection, so that part grows with the members, not with a constant.
- So the cap has a part that grows with the limit, which your twice covers, and a fixed part, the about 54 MB a relay holds before anyone connects. On a big relay that fixed part is negligible, as you say; on a tiny one it is most of the memory.
- Both together: the cap is twice the limit plus 64 MB. At 256 that is 576; at 32 it is 128, so a tiny relay is not killed; at 2 GB it is about 4.1 GB.
- The large end then belongs to the raise check: since the cap is what the box must really have, a raise passes only when the cap's growth, not the limit's, fits in what the box has free. A 2 GB relay on a 4 GB box is then refused, which is right.
- ? Twice plus 64, and the raise checked by the cap's growth?

the cap is is much more tied to the number of member we serve simultaneously the the almost negligible amount the node itself uses. that seems to be fact to me, we're better off computing the cap of number of members we allow, that that bit of other overhead....

- cw: agreed, the cap follows the members the relay admits. In numbers, from noderoutes' own report at 256 MB:
  - it admits 1,077 members, three connections each, 3,232 in all;
  - each connection is budgeted at 64 KB of the relay's own memory, so the members take about 202 MB of the 256;
  - the other 54 MB is what the relay holds with nobody connected.
- So the cap is: the members' share counted twice, once for the relay and once for the kernel's buffers, about 404 MB, plus the 54 MB at rest. About 458 MB in all.
- One flag, said once: the 54 MB is not negligible at this size, it is a fifth of a 256 MB relay. A cap without it would be 404 MB, while a full relay really needs about 458, so systemd would kill it just before it is full. On a large relay it fades, as you say, but it never hurts to count it.
- ? The cap as the members' share twice plus what the relay holds at rest?
wsl?

- wsl: agreed with cw: the cap counted from the members it admits, twice their share plus what it holds at rest, about 458 MB at 256. The "twice" is our model of the kernel's buffers, not a measurement, so the relay should report its real service figure beside it and we check the model against noderoutes and spirit-3.
- How the relay moves its own cap: it runs as root under systemd, so one call, systemctl set-property <unit> MemoryMax=<cap>, changes it live and keeps it across restarts, no reinstall.
- ? That call, on every limit change, as the way the relay moves its cap?

what I'm trying to say, to simplify the fucking number, is: the cap must be twice the size of what we compute for relay-internal use, per member, so for a 256MB not as computed today the cap must be 512MB, simple, AND safe.

agreed?

- cw: agreed, and it is safer than my sum. The relay's allowance is already worked out from its limit less what it holds at rest: (256 less 54) at 16 connections a MB is exactly the 3,232 in noderoutes' report. So the limit already holds both parts, and twice it, 512, is above the 458 a full relay needs.
- That also answers my worry about tiny relays: the at-rest part is inside the limit, so it is doubled too.
- Boxed, your words with it, in place of the old limit plus 128.
- One consequence: what the box must really have is the cap, so a raise from 256 to 512 asks the box for 512 more, not 256. That is the raise check counting the cap's growth, which is twice the difference.
so realisticly on a 1GB VPS that's empty, a relay should never allot more than 384MB for itself....

- wsl: close, a little lower: with the cap at twice the limit, 384 makes a 768 MB cap, and Caddy (about 100 to 200) plus the system (about 100 to 150) take it past 1,024.
- The edge is about 350 MB (700 cap + about 275 beside it); the 256 you recommend leaves about a quarter spare.
- So: never more than about 350 on an empty 1 GB VPS, and 256 recommended. The raise check, counting the cap's growth against what is free, refuses past that edge by itself.
yes, but my bet is this: we will never have all 1000 member use the relay at full throttle ever....

- cw: very likely right, and the cap costs nothing in that case: it is a ceiling, not a reservation. Linux sets nothing aside for it, so whatever the relay does not use stays free for Caddy and the system.
- The cap and the limit only matter at the peak you bet against. What they decide there is who goes down: with the cap, systemd stops the relay alone and it restarts in seconds; without one, the box runs out and the kernel kills whatever it picks, Caddy or the SSH you would need to fix it.
- So on an empty 1 GB VPS, 384 is a fair bet that usually wins, and 256 is the figure that cannot lose. The recommendation stays 256, as you ruled, and the raise check lets an owner take the bet up to about 350 if he wants it.

items.title: Root test folder in spirit/run
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Make spirit.js what it is supposed to be (goal/G40).

RULE ONE, ALL CODE (Andy, 2026-10-24)
- spirit.js is the only JavaScript client interface to the SpiritOS core.
- Every module and page loads spirit.js first and does everything through it.

SCOPE (Andy, 2026-10-24): "all we do, is: replace duplicate hand-rolled shit with the use of spirit.js, no other stuff, no new desk button no new verbs, just kill removeAgent".

THE DESIGN
1. One instance per VM. On a page it is window.spirit; in node it is the only export of spirit.js, the same object for every module that requires it. Nothing makes a second one: no createSpirit, assemble, forNode or forPeer.
2. Where it runs: isNode() and isBrowser(), in spirit.js and nowhere else. Then, always in this order (Andy, 2026-10-25: "spirit.js is loaded, it then check node/browser, then if browser it check loopback/not-loopback, then decides what more to fetch"): in a browser, a loopback page is on its home node, any other page is a face reached through a relay; from that spirit.js decides what more to fetch. Through a relay: the face shell from the relay, and, once linked, the seal from the home node.
3. Its node. On a page, the page's own origin. In node, 127.0.0.1 and the port spirit.js reads from relay-state/environment.json whenever it is required. Only a server listening on a loopback port writes that port, and only serveCommon writes it (writeEnvironment, called by the node at its start, before any server process starts). Andy: "it really belongs in serverCommon." No port, no node: never a default.
4. One post and one get, nothing else reaches the node. post(verb, args) sends {verb, ...args} to the node's /api/spirit; get(path) fetches a file. On a face both go through the face's link to its home node, which spirit.js owns. A peer is asked by one post too, the node's peer.post.
5. The node's families on the instance: spirit.<family>.<verb>(args), each a function that checks its arguments against the family's api.js and then posts. The families are what the node names; each is bound on the instance.
6. spirit.require(path, key): the one loader, the same on a page and in node. A component by its run-root path (in node required, on a page got and run); an interface binds its family on the instance; with a key, the peer's family.
6a. Every loaded or required module inserts its own api functions into the one instance (Andy, 2026-10-24: "every loaded/required module then simply inserts its api functions into the one spirit object"): a component as it loads, a node family's api.js as spirit.js runs it.
7. Its helpers: error, formatBytes, escapeHtml, check, rules, outcome. No spirit.call (Andy, 2026-10-24: "just kill it. i see absolutely no need for it."): a caller holding a verb in a variable writes spirit[family][verb](args). In node spirit.js loads no kernel: the node's facts, the job, peerPost, VERSION, DEFAULT_SPIRIT_PORT, MIME_TYPES and debug are its own; the node and the relay load no kernel.js either (fileSystem.js, serveCommon.readBody, jobs.js its own state).
8. face.html holds spirit.js alone; spirit.js loads the seal and face/shell.js; face/shell.js keeps only drawing and opening apps.

THE EVENTS FAMILY (Andy, 2026-10-25: "two verbs on events - publish - subscribe"): /api/events, a door outside any api, becomes spirit/events/, a family like fs, owner only on the loopback table. It is the node's one dispatcher: the jobs, the relay events, the packets and the contact renames feed it; its subscribers are the node's pages, its processes and the owner's face (through faceHome). events.subscribe: what is known now, then every event with its kind. events.publish: a server's object to every subscriber, in place of writing it onto its job. On a page spirit.events.subscribe and publish, on spirit.js's one get and one post; the kernel's page stream goes.

ONE PATH TO PUBLISH (Andy, 2026-10-25: "from now on. ONE path for everybody to publish events. decision. and don't come later and say that i never said that."): every publisher, appServer's stream publisher and every server alike, publishes through spirit.events.publish and nothing else; appServer's publish adds only its fan-out to its own subscribers.

localReview and localResearch ARE DELETED (Andy, 2026-10-25: "KILL THEM.").

removeAgent.js IS DELETED, and nothing replaces it: no verb, no button (Andy, 2026-10-24: "just KILL remove agent, I can manually revoke an agents access to desk").

DONE WHEN spirit.js can replace every hand-rolled interface provider: face/shell.js's link, jobs subscription and part loader; kernel.js's page interfaces; appServer.js and appClient.js for the processes; the own fetches of localResearch and localReview; index.html's loading of its 54 scripts.

THE RED: spirit/run/test/spirit.js, the only one, asserting spirit/run/test/spirit.md (written from spirit.js: rule one, its role, every function, the one interface, the one loader, red when spirit.js is not loaded first). Every function tested in node and on a page. No new desk tests, and no other new suite but one: a single throw-away test in spirit/test/ that makes sure spirit.js works wherever it is put to use (Andy, 2026-10-24: "we test spirit.js and then we make sure it works wherever we put it. you can make one throw-away test for that, where all the other hundred junk tests are."). The old suites are not run for this item.

KEPT FROM e0709bd6: the test tree (spirit/run/test/ core; test/<name>.md, <name>.js, -child-, -sibling-), testModule.js, the general rules, runAll through testModule.

cw: yes. To be precise about who the man in the middle is:
- Not someone on the wire: home to relay and relay to face both run over https, so an outsider cannot read or change it.
- The relay itself is the middle. A relay run by someone hostile, or broken into, can change anything it passes on unsealed: seal.js, and worse, the home keys the face asks for before sealing. - What closes it: home signs the bytes of everything it sends, the keys answer above all, and the face checks each against home's public key. items.title: face bugs
items.creator: andy
items.box:
FACE BUGS, and the rules the face is built to.

THE RULES (Andy, 2026-10-25):
- The contained app: the window is the screen and the page never scrolls; below the title bar the app area takes the rest; an app's tools never scroll; only a list or a viewer scrolls, inside itself.
- Space is granted top-down: whoever mounts an element hands it a box of set size, and it lays out only inside it. No element sizes itself.
- probabilitySearch is the one list. In list mode: filters, then the search row, fixed; the list the rest, scrolling, its current row kept in view; up, down, home, end, page up and page down on the whole list. listSearch is deprecated and forbidden in the face.
- The header element is deprecated: a tool bar is an app's first row.
- Shell-app state lives in relay-state/shell/<app>/, out of git; system sets in shell/json/ (core), updated by hand.
- A change goes to the server and every view hears it on the stream; nothing hands a result back.

BUILT (d5a41760 .. b41d0459):
- No app script reads the kernel, so the face can open any of them; spirit.relay.status is the relay family's.
- listSearch, the contact selector and the header element are off the face; the marking rule is in probabilitySearch.
- The list keys and scroll as above; face.css makes the face a contained app; shell.css .fill is the box a mounter hands down (Files, Icons, Apps, Contacts).
- Icons: the owner's set in relay-state/shell/icons/iconSet.json, else shell/json/iconSet.json; the picker offers the system set; the node opens relay-state/shell/<app>/ and the folders to it, nothing else under relay-state; shell/json/ is core.

TO BUILD, NAVIGATION:
- The face shell's stack holds pages only: a page is a title and something that draws into a box. An app is a desktop icon whose click pushes its page; a detail is a page its app pushes.
- The frame owns the title bar: the top page's title, and back, which pops it; home pops them all. Every page gets the whole app area.
- A popped page is thrown away; the one under it stays as it was. A page may close itself.
- No results on the stack: the 13 hand-backs and the two callers reading them go. The icon detail saves to the server; the file watcher's notice comes back, and the Icons list fetches the file again.
- A navigationWrapper shell element in shell/js/: it pushes a page, puts its title and back in the title bar, and hands the page the whole app area.
- The shell does all the wrapping: opening an app pushes its page through the navigationWrapper with the app's name and mount, and the app only draws into the box it is handed; a detail goes through the same wrapper. No app wraps itself.
- natterDetails and contactsDetails go as apps; they become intrinsic shell elements in shell/js/, built on the navigationWrapper, no manifests, no callDialog. Icons pushes its icon detail through it. The old shell is not touched.
- In this item, no new items (Andy: "this is hopefully the last round for this one").

items.title: Make face run on both: loopback AND relay
items.creator: andy
items.box:
THE MAILED LINK NAMES ITS RELAY (Andy, 2026-10-25: "this email does not specify the router-ID to which my email confirmation is supposed to go. so my node 65432 always tries spirit.andyflinn.com and always fails."; "box it."): the relay writes its own address into the link, /face.html?join=<code>&relay=<its url>&app=join, and the face sends the code to that relay, never to the first relay the node lists. A relay and face change, so a tag.

INFO'S FIXES (Andy, 2026-10-25):
- The foot goes whole, the key and its sentence ("fine-print at the bottom. nobody read that shit, and it doesn't help anybody."); no key shows in Info, as no key shows anywhere (goal/G40.1).
- The email form is in Info itself, above the face form: the shell element joinForm, as the relay details draw it for a seated member (Andy: "isn't the email-change bit on the relay-details a shell-element as well? it should also be placed in info, above the face-pick-interface...."); no words sending you to Natter, which is gone.
- In Info it comes with a relay picker, the element's general form (Andy: "in info, it needs a replay picker with it, (the general form of that element), but we learned now that all things relay need association with the relays ID..... unless they show up in a detail-page for a specific relay."). EVERY RELAY THING NAMES ITS RELAY: a form, a link or a call about a relay carries that relay's id, unless it sits on that relay's own details page. There the picker shows as a reminder, fixed, with its one option (Andy: "on the relays detail page the picker CAN be shown as a reminder, but unchangeable, with only one option.").
- ONE PICKER PER FORM: the forms are atomic, each with its own relay picker, the same form from Join to the relay details to Info (Andy: "one each. those forms are atomic. no optimization, it will make things complicated, because: i have an email on one relay, but not the other etc... and that way the form itself can always show up in a familiar form, from the join app all the way to relay details AND the info panel.").
- ONE FORM, ONE LINE, EVERYWHERE (Andy: "the form is: [relay-dropdown] [email-adress-input] [change-or-join] the SAME FUCKING FORM EVERYWHERE, DAMMIT-."): the relay dropdown, the email address and the Join or Change button side by side, in Join, in the relay details (the dropdown fixed to that relay, its one option) and in Info. THE ORDER (Andy: "First fix the form, then place the form everywhere with the correct options"): first the form itself, joinForm, becomes that one row with its dropdown; then every place draws that one form, each with its options: Join and Info every relay this node is on, the relay details its one relay, fixed.
- THE FACE FORM THE SAME (Andy: "same with the face form."): one row, [relay dropdown] [face name] [Ask], first fixed as a form, then drawn in Join, Info and the relay details with their options, the relay details its one relay, fixed.
- THE FACE FORM'S RELAYS (Andy: "for a face form: doesn't show up if the user has zero verified emails anywhere; only shows relay in the dropdown, where the user has a confirmed email address. THAT's WHY THE FORMS HAVE SEPARATE RELAY DROPDOWNS."): its dropdown lists only the relays where this node's email is verified, and with none anywhere the face form does not show.
- The relay table says what each relay calls you: a relay you own seats you at boot (goal/G30.7), and your node notes that seat under the relay's name for you when the relay reports to you.

NO KEYS IN ANY USER INTERFACE (Andy, 2026-10-25: "remove ANY indication of keys from all user interfaces, like that footer on the info app"): no key, whole or in part, is shown in any face app ("just all face-apps, the legacy stuff doesn't interest me.").

NO NAMELESS ROWS IN CONTACTS (Andy, 2026-10-25: "box them"): the list shows no row without a name. Today it shows two on a new node, the relay's own key and the node's own key, because the presence data seats every key a relay reports present, whether or not it is a person to add.

FIELDS THAT KEEP THEIR LIMIT (Andy, 2026-10-25: "input field with fieldRules.js limit keep counting the number of characters typed beyond the limit, instead of just blocking input past the limit"; "no fieldRules.js for emails?"; "malformed email address say: "type your email address" ??????"; "254"):
- Every field with a fieldRules limit stops taking input at its limit, counted in bytes; its count says only what is left, never how many too many.
- fieldRules.js has an email rule: one address, one @, a domain, at most 254 bytes; the forms and the node use that one rule.
- A malformed address is told what is wrong with it, from that rule.

THE RELAYS ON THE STREAM (Andy, 2026-10-25: "why would my node not stream a change in relay status?"; "box it."): the node publishes its relay rows (seat, email, verified, face, each relay) on the stream whenever one changes; Info and both forms redraw from that, so a join or a face finished anywhere reaches every open screen.

THE MAILED LINK IS THE PAGE THAT ASKED (Andy, 2026-10-25: "USE THE FUCKING URL that triggered, the join", and "the node DOES know where the address came from. now we just have to fix it in the least-dirty way"): the node knows where a join was asked from, its own loopback page or the face the call came through, and hands that address with the join; the relay mails its link there, with the code and its own key. The mail is read anywhere, so a join asked from a face gets a link that opens anywhere.
- THE SHAPE (Andy, 2026-10-25, line by line: agreed, then "WOW. proceed."): the first call carries {email, URL, card}, URL being the caller's link, the link the shell wants opened, app part and all; only the shell knows it. The relay adds the code as a GET argument and its key as the last GET argument, and mails it: <URL>&join=<code>&relay=<key>. The second call stays {code, card}: the relay holds the email under the node's key for those 10 minutes. The relay knows no loopback, no port, no page and no app name. The face shell reads the join link on a relay face too, after its login.

WHAT A FACE MAY NOT ASK (Andy, 2026-10-25: "when did i rule that face cannot call relay.join?", and "i can see the point of refusing to change the face name for the face I'm calling from. THAT's different."): a face may join and change its email through relay.join like the local shell. The one thing refused is changing the face name on the relay the face is called through, by relay.face or by a post carrying a face name to that relay. A face name on any other relay may be asked from the face.

items.title: One table for all known IDs
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
ONE TABLE FOR ALL KNOWN IDS (Andy, 2026-10-25 and 26)

THE TABLE
- seen, the shadow in node.db, is the one table. contacts.json, the relays table and the peers table move into it and go. The grants table stays its own, keyed by ID.
- One row per ID other than the node itself, size-capped, kept current by the relay streams.
- Every row: label (with how sure and when), myLabel, card, present, firstSeen, lastSeen.
- Booleans on every row: keep, mine, relay, held, ignored, blocked, seated. choice and kind go.
- Gone: acquiredVia, memberOf, missingSince, cardVia, cardDisputed; from the relays table listed, pos, acceptedAt, replaced, seatLabel, seatClaimedAt, refusal, refusedAt, faceName, faceEmail, faceReply, email, emailVerified.

ROUTES
- seen_routes stays, per ID: via, url, when, rank, told. The contacts' own relay and route lists move into it.
- A URL is a route: an ID's own address, a relay's or a node's on a LAN, is a direct route through no relay.
- The route is the pin. The check stays in answerRelay: an answer from a URL must come from the ID whose route it is; a new one is accepted, a different one refused and reported. One lookup, on an index over the routes' url.

MEANINGS
- keep: a chosen contact, never shed. mine: owned, puppets and owned relays, never shed. relay: the ID is a relay. held: waits for your yes. ignored: politely refused, no reason given, never shown. blocked: refused, a relay as well as a node.
- seated: that ID holds this node, a relay its seat, a node its chosen contacts. Set by any post it carried or answered, cleared by a refusal as no member. Nothing else of a seat is stored.
- The node stores no email: it is given only to take a seat. A member's row on a relay is always pushed by the member, so the relay need not tell the node who it is; no seat verb.
- Home is every relay this node is seated on. The relays shown on screens are the relays kept.
- A card is valid only signed by the row's ID; any other is refused and nothing of it kept.
- lastSeen is the staleness: it orders shedding once the cap is reached, never age alone. Shedding takes unflagged rows first, then ignored or blocked, then held, oldest first in each; keep and mine never.

INDEXES
- A partial index per flag, holding only the rows where it is true, and one over the rows with neither keep nor mine, by lastSeen.

SEARCH
- One verb over the one table replaces contact.search and relay.search: words ranked as now; kept and held rows only; yes-filters keep, mine, relay, seated, held, blocked; each boolean a mark on its row in Contacts.
- What the network search finds is held: a search is your look at its results, so each find waits for your yes like any held row.

THE STREAM: one job for the table, one changed row per update, never the whole table.

THE MOVE: on each node's first start on the new code, contacts.json, the relays table and the peers table go into the one table, then are deleted. One tag; the relays do not move.

GRANTED FOR THIS ITEM: verb changes and removals, table changes and removals.

- Storage: in node.db the relays, peers and seen tables (and seen_routes beside seen) become one table with its routes; every node's rows move over on its first start, contacts and seats kept. One tag, a flag day.
- Core modules: four, about 2,100 lines, become one: relayKeys (608), contacts (668), seenPeers (339), ownerBadge (527), on nodeStore's schema.
- Their callers, all core: hub (about 100 calls), peerPost, presenceNode, server, apiAuth, answerRelay, nodeCard, joinStepsJob, relayRowsJob.
- Not touched, if contact.* and relay.* keep their answers: the shell, the face, every app, and the relays (their members table is their own).

Approach
- pick the db-table that is going to be THE ONE, figure out what it already has, and what it needs to support all features we have so far.

- THE ONE: seen, the shadow, in node.db. Keyed by ID, capped, shed by staleness, fed by the relay streams; already a target of peerPost. Today 49 rows on your node.
- It has: publicKey, label (with how sure and when), seen (last heard, for shedding), present, choice, blocked, kind (node or relay). Beside it seen_routes: ID, via which relay, url, rank, told.
- Four stores hold the same IDs today, not three: seen; contacts.json (a file, 5 rows on your node); the relays table (4 rows); and the peers table (6 rows, IDs holding grants, beside the grants table).
- What seen lacks, from contacts.json: remember (your contacts), mine (owned, your puppets), myLabel (your own name for it), its card and cardVia, acquiredVia, memberOf, missingSince. Its relays and routes fit seen_routes.
- What seen lacks, from the relays table, for a row of kind relay: url (its address), listed and pos (your relay list and its order), the key's pin history (firstSeen, acceptedAt, replaced), your seat (seatLabel, seatClaimedAt), the relay's refusal (refusal, refusedAt), your face there (faceName, faceEmail, faceReply), your email there (email, emailVerified).
- The peers table: one label per ID that holds a grant; seen has the label already. The grants table (ID by path) stays its own, keyed by ID.
- So seen gains two flags and about 18 columns, and the shed sweep spares any row with remember or mine.
- Correction, counted: two flags and 21 columns (6 from contacts.json, 15 from the relays table), not about 18.
is staleness an alternate key/timestamp of last-touched?

- Yes: a timestamp, not a key. The column seen holds when the ID was last heard of (milliseconds), with its own index, seen_when; the key stays the ID.
- It only orders who goes first when the table is full: no row goes for age alone (your 0021: "I don't see why the node should throw away memories when the 20 Megabyte cap is not exhausted yet").
- And I missed one thing it has: the choice mark. A row marked added and not blocked is never shed; then held, then ignored or blocked, oldest first. So remember exists already as choice added; mine (owned) is the flag still missing.

- relay: the column kind already says node or relay. A boolean would say the same twice; I would keep kind and drop the idea of a relay flag, unless you want more kinds than two never.
- What choice still carries beside added: held (a contact you took in but do not listen to yet) and ignored (someone who wrote, turned away); blocked is its own boolean already. Do held and ignored stay, as booleans too, or go?

what is pin history? listed and pos?

- Pin history: which key this node trusts for that relay's address. The first key that answered there is pinned (firstSeen, acceptedAt); if a different key ever answers at the same address, the node refuses it until accepted, and replaced keeps the key it took over from. It is what stops someone else standing at spirit's address.
- listed: the relay is on your relay list (the relays in Contacts, Info, the forms). A relay can be unlisted and still keep its pinned key, so a later add knows it.
- pos: its place in that list; the first listed is the node's home relay, the one it falls back to.
explain: "which key this node trusts for that relay's address"

- A relay is reached at an address, https://spirit.andyflinn.com, but it is who it is by its ID, its key. Anyone who gets hold of that address (a DNS trick, a hijacked box) could answer there.
- So the first time your node talks to that address, it writes down the ID that answered, beside the address. After that, every answer from that address must come from that same ID; a different ID answering there is refused. That is the pin: this address belongs to this ID.
- In the one table it gets simpler: the row is the relay's ID, its URL is a route on that row, and the pin is just when that route was accepted (acceptedAt) and which ID the address belonged to before, if it ever changed (replaced).

- Yes, it is there already: the row is the ID, its URL a route on it. That IS the pin; it needs no columns of its own.
- What stays is the check, as behaviour: an answer from that URL must come from the row's ID, or it is refused. firstSeen is the row's own already.

- Today that is one row, keyed by ID, unique on url: one lookup, two fields on the same row, no second field to compare.
- In the one table the same: find the row whose route is that URL, compare its ID with the key that answered. One lookup on an index over the routes' url. The check stays where it is; only its two helpers read the one table.

items.box:
the first set of changes i propose
- 1. You can turn design on for an item at any time.
- 2. No commit lands while the current goal, or the item the agent is on, is in design mode, granted or not.
- 3. all searches in desk are of the new probability variety.
- 4. the rules get a new "test" type. all rules get a field that indicates "auto-attach-at-goal-creation-time"
- 5. The desk sends no idle question at all (the stale-Q code is gone since 03858cf9, and nothing replaces it).
- 6. An agent raises ONE red Q when a decision blocks its progress; that Q is then discussed.
- 7. Reopening an item or a goal puts it back into design.
- 8. A build and a verify run the item's red only (rule/10), and rule/10 rides on build and verify by default.

second set of changes
- 1. each goal and item gets a list of attached rules.
- 2. the icons strip to the left of a goal has an icon for the list of attached rules
- 3. rules can be added with a propabilitySearch-dropdown for rules and they can be remove from the goal/item with a delete button on the rule-row
- 4. during design, attached "design" rules will accompany every wake-up for the agent.
- 5 during red phase, attached "test" rules to item and goal accompany the successful take of the red phase, and all wakes of the test-writing agent during the red phase. Verify falls under the test rules too: they accompany the take of verify and its wakes.
- 6. the equivalent for "code" phase. a successful take of "code" will be accompanied by "code" rules attached to "code" item and goal. (The code phase is today's build.)
- 7. The rules attached to an agent's work are the goal's rules for the current phase plus the current item's, each once.
- 8. The desk client caches the rule attachments of the current goal and its items; the desk pushes them only when an attachment changes, so a wake carries no rule text it already holds.
- 9. "desk" rules ALWAYS accompany every wake of an agent! We aggreed on it, but it didn't make the box

items.title: Fix contacts UI
items.creator: wsl-claude
items.box:
FIX THE CONTACTS UI
- The Contacts page hands its list a box of a stated size: the page is a flex column, and the list box takes the shell's fill class, as in Apps and Icons. The panels below it keep their own height.
- The rule against the regression, type ui: a page that mounts a list element hands it a box it has sized itself; an element never sizes its own box (rule/16).

THE PRODUCT TEST SYSTEM
- 1. It lives in spirit/run/test/ and depends on nothing outside spirit/run/. Nothing of it reaches into spirit/test/ at all. It provides its own support there, so it never needs spirit/test/: its reporter prints the same lines as today, so the verifier reads it unchanged, and when the verifier started the run it posts each result to the node's verifier through the spirit object, as every module does.
- 2. testModule.js in spirit/run/test/ finds every test of the product tree, and names the tests a changed file needs. The old run-all only calls it.
- 3. Tests sit beside the module. A folder's ./test/ holds, for every module ./<name>.js in that folder, ./test/<name>.js (the tests of that module only) and ./test/<name>.md (its precise specification). A page such as index.html gets its pair there too. spirit/run/test/ does this for spirit.js today.
- 4. A test exercises its module as its .md specifies: it drives it, stresses it and tries to break it.
- 5. A module without its own test is left alone, so the tree comes in one module at a time. Deprecated legacy code gets none.

THE DESK
- 6. When a file on an item's file list is in the product tree and has its own test, that test joins the item's test list by itself. Nobody lists it by hand.
- 7. Once a file in spirit/run/shell/ is on the item, all auto-attach ui rules are attached to the item. The ui rules attached to an item ride on every take and every wake. Auto-attach ui rules never come at goal creation: a new goal cannot tell yet whether it will touch the UI.

THE VERIFIER
- 8. The verifier runs product tests: the paths under spirit/run/ that testModule.js names, beside those under spirit/test/.
- 9. The verifier UI has a button that runs the full product test tree.
- 10. The verifier tab opens at any time, also while tests are running.

THIS ITEM
- 11. Test pairs first for the modules the Contacts face-app uses: contacts/listElement, contacts/rowElement, contacts/data, probabilitySearch, rowElement, spiritData and contactLabel.
- 12. The face-approved shell/js elements, each to get its pair, not necessarily in this item: probabilitySearch, rowElement, spiritData, navigationWrapper, textView, textViewer, fieldInput, joinForm, faceForm, joinSteps, contactLabel, fileViewer and mediaViewer.

- The fix: #contacts-book becomes fill, and the folding panels below it sit outside that box, so the list takes what the pane leaves.

- cw: the cause: Contacts hands the search a box with no size. Its list box is a plain tile, and the page is not a column that gives it the height left over.
- Apps and Icons do it right: the list box takes the shell's fill class (a flex box that takes the space left and shrinks to it), inside a page that is a flex column. G40.8 fixed Files and Icons that way; Contacts was never touched.
- The fix: the Contacts page becomes a flex column, its list box takes fill, and the two panels under it (Add a relay, People who write) keep their own height below it.
- The rule I propose, type ui: Space is granted top-down. A page that mounts a list element hands it a box it has sized itself (fill, in a flex column); an element never sizes its own box, and a page never hands over a box without a size.
